name: Patisiran
route_note: IV infusion every three weeks after premedication

discovery.note: A double-stranded siRNA against a conserved sequence in the transthyretin mRNA 3' untranslated region, encapsulated in lipid nanoparticles that deliver it to the liver.

tagline: First approved RNA interference drug, silencing transthyretin in hereditary amyloidosis
summary: Patisiran is a lipid nanoparticle-formulated small interfering RNA that silences transthyretin production in the liver. In 2018 it became the first RNA interference therapeutic to be approved, for polyneuropathy of hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis.
mechanism: Transthyretin (TTR) is a liver-made transport protein. Mutations destabilise its tetramer, and misfolded monomers deposit as amyloid in nerves and heart.

Patisiran's lipid nanoparticles acquire apolipoprotein E in blood and are taken up by hepatocytes via LDL receptors. Inside, the siRNA loads into the RNA-induced silencing complex, which cleaves TTR mRNA, reducing serum TTR by about 80% and slowing or reversing neuropathy progression.
uses: Polyneuropathy of hereditary transthyretin-mediated (hATTR) amyloidosis in adults

history.title: RNA interference
history.detail: Andrew Fire and Craig Mello describe RNA interference in worms, recognised with the 2006 Nobel Prize.

history.title: Alnylam founded
history.detail: Alnylam is founded to develop RNAi therapeutics.

history.title: APOLLO trial
history.detail: Patisiran improves neuropathy and quality of life versus placebo in hATTR amyloidosis.

history.title: First RNAi approval
history.detail: FDA approves Onpattro in August; the EU approves it the same month.

history.title: Vutrisiran
history.detail: Alnylam's subcutaneous successor vutrisiran is approved for hATTR polyneuropathy.

history.title: Cardiomyopathy declined
history.detail: FDA issues a complete response letter for patisiran in ATTR cardiomyopathy despite APOLLO-B results.

facts: Premedication with a corticosteroid, paracetamol and antihistamines is required to reduce infusion reactions.
